strengths: The central idea is clean and well-motivated: the paper deduces (rather than assumes) a local port–Hamiltonian factorization for mesh dynamics from four principles (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, passivity), making the topology–metric split a consequence of the theory rather than a prescribed template. This is a genuine conceptual contribution over postulated global Hamiltonian/port-Hamiltonian templates.

The supporting theory is developed carefully: the appendix gives a complete proof chain (Lemmas A.1–A.4), including the skew/dissipative split from incremental energy conditions and the signed-incidence wiring result, plus a corollary on state-independent interconnections and a Maxwell example showing that discrete divergence invariants (D_{k+1}D_k = 0) are preserved by construction.

The ablation study (Table 9, Appendix C.7) is unusually well aligned with the theory: each variant selectively violates one assumption (orientation, topology, metric positivity, learned-J), and the empirical outcomes match the theoretical predictions. This substantially strengthens the claim that the structural assumptions matter.

Efficiency is impressive: MeshFT-Net has only ~642 parameters, uses O(N) sparse operations, and Table 10 shows it is fastest and most memory-efficient while attaining the best TSMSE across resolutions.

OOD generalization experiments (frequency, resolution, wave-speed shifts, Table 4/8) are a valuable addition, and the data-efficiency analysis (Figs. 2 and 4) supports the inductive-bias claim. Code, configurations, and seeds are promised and supplementary materials are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claims. The main benchmarks are essentially linear plane-wave problems, for which the quadratic MeshFT-Net model is exactly in the true hypothesis class. The strong wins (near-zero one-step MSE, near-zero energy drift) are therefore partly by construction: the architecture matches the data-generating process, while baselines do not. The headline 'near-zero energy drift' comparisons are close to tautological, since MeshFT-Net conserves its energy analytically.

The 'realistic' validation is thin. The only non-synthetic experiment (The Well acoustic scattering) reports qualitative snapshots of a single model with no baseline comparison or quantitative metrics in the main text, so the abstract's claim of strong results on 'realistic datasets' is under-supported. There is no nonlinear PDE benchmark of practical scale; the nonlinear check is a small shallow-water-style toy with only 4 training trajectories.

Novelty relative to prior structure-preserving work needs sharper delineation. The topology–metric split is classical in DEC, FDTD, and finite-element exterior calculus, and fixing incidence operators while learning discrete Hodge stars is close to data-driven exterior calculus (Trask et al., 2022), which the paper acknowledges. The practical realization (quadratic storage + KDK stepping) largely recovers a discretized wave solver with learned Hodge operators; the main differentiator is the principle-driven derivation, which is a formalization contribution rather than a new capability.

Some proof details are under-argued. In Lemma A.4 the positivity of the diagonal gains C_k is asserted via 'an orientation gauge choice' without a rigorous argument, and the statement that skew-symmetry forces the two off-diagonal blocks to share per-incidence weights glosses over cases where a (k, k+1) incidence structure admits more than the ideal signed-incidence pattern.

Presentation issues: several typos ('metrix' for 'matrix' on p.5, 'though' for 'through' in Appendix B, 'relying the reduction theorem' in the conclusion), formatting problems in Table 3 (e.g., '9.999 96 × 10−1'), and no dedicated limitations section discussing scope restrictions (e.g., fixed topology, linear/quadratic storage, sources handled only additively).

Baseline fairness is adequate on hyperparameters but baselines are described as 'pedagogically clear' choices; stronger structure-preserving competitors from the port-Hamiltonian/neural-constitutive literature are discussed in related work but not compared against empirically.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized: the topology–metric separation idea is motivating, the reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) is stated precisely, and a complete proof is supplied in Appendix A with supporting lemmas.

The architecture (MeshFT-Net) follows directly from the theory: fixing the signed-incidence interconnection and learning only SPD metric/PSD dissipation operators is a clean, principled design, and Algorithm 1 with Strang splitting and CFL guard is a sensible instantiation.

The ablation study in Appendix C.7 (Table 9) is genuinely informative: selectively violating orientation, topology, and metric positivity degrades long-horizon stability and momentum conservation, empirically supporting each component of the theorem.

Breadth of evaluation is reasonable for the setting: analytic plane waves on grids and Delaunay meshes, a dissipative benchmark, physics-consistency diagnostics (Table 3), OOD shifts (Table 4), a nonlinear toy system, and computational cost analysis (Table 10), with multiple seeds reported.

A useful Maxwell example (Appendix B) shows how spurious modes are eliminated by the incidence-wired interconnection, and Table 10 suggests the method is very lightweight (642 parameters) relative to baselines.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core theorem. Lemma A.3 is essentially standard port–Hamiltonian algebra (incremental passivity conditions imply a skew/dissipative Jacobian split), and Lemma A.4 (locality + permutation equivariance confine linear maps to incidence operators) is close to known DEC results the authors themselves cite (Hirani; Desbrun et al.; Trask et al.). The 'deduced rather than assumed' framing is overstated: Assumption 3.2(E) already posits a conservative–dissipative split and pointwise energy balance, so much of the port–Hamiltonian structure is built into the hypotheses rather than derived from them.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claims. The main quantitative benchmarks are linear wave equations on periodic domains—a setting where the fixed incidence interconnection exactly matches the true dynamics—so MeshFT-Net is essentially evaluated on its own model class. The one 'realistic' experiment (The Well acoustic scattering) reports only qualitative snapshots with no baseline comparison or quantitative metrics in the paper, so the claim of strong fidelity on realistic data is not well supported.

Baseline fairness is questionable. MGN/HNN baselines have ~10^5 parameters versus 642 for MeshFT-Net, yet MGN's one-step MSE (Table 1) is two orders of magnitude worse than a 642-parameter model on a linear wave—suggesting undertrained or misconfigured baselines rather than a fundamental advantage of the proposed structure. More competitive structure-preserving baselines from the cited literature (e.g., weak-form/port-Hamiltonian approaches, Trask et al.'s data-driven DEC) are described in Related Work but not compared against.

The momentum-conservation claim ('preserved without an explicit constraint') is a direct algebraic consequence of the chosen incidence wiring, not an empirical discovery; presenting it as an experimental finding (Table 3) inflates the contribution.

The theory assumes state-independent metric/incidence gains (Corollary 3.4) for the main experiments, which restricts applicability to linear media; the state-dependent extension is only probed on a small toy example (Section 5.5). Limitations regarding nonlinear PDEs, sources, and discontinuous media are discussed only obliquely, and there is no dedicated limitations section.

Some presentation issues: 'metrix' (typo) in Section 4, and inconsistencies between the headline claim of 'near-zero energy drift' and Table 6/Appendix numbers (e.g., 7.2×10^-3), which are small but not near-zero.

strengths: The central idea is clean and well-motivated: separating topological (incidence-fixed) from metric-dependent (learnable) structure in mesh-based learned dynamics, formalized as a local reduction theorem rather than postulated as a template. The Maxwell example (Appendix C) nicely shows that discrete Gauss constraints emerge as exact structural invariants rather than soft penalties.

The theory is worked out carefully: Lemmas B.1–B.4 give a complete proof chain from locality + permutation equivariance + orientation covariance to signed-incidence wiring, and the paper is honest about what the theorem does and does not claim (equation-agnostic, local, piecewise-smooth regions).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough and well-aligned with the theory: analytic plane-wave and dissipative benchmarks, model-agnostic physics-consistency diagnostics (dispersion, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum), OOD shifts in frequency/speed/resolution, transfer to The Well acoustic scattering, irregular heterogeneous elasticity, nonlinear lattice systems, runtime/memory scaling, and principle-level ablations (Table 14) that selectively violate each theorem assumption.

The ablations are a decisive strength: they empirically separate the roles of orientation, incidence topology, and metric positivity, directly supporting the theoretical claims (e.g., scrambled topology causes energy drift despite one-step MSE remaining small).

MeshFT-Net is extremely parameter- and memory-efficient (642 params vs. ~10^5 for baselines) while achieving better long-horizon behavior and lower energy drift; this makes the inductive-bias story concrete and practically relevant.

Reproducibility appears good: code is stated to be released, hyperparameters and data generation procedures are documented in detail in Appendices D.1–D.7, and results are reported as means over multiple seeds.
weaknesses: The reduction theorem has a partial circularity concern. Lemma B.3 derives the (J, R) factorization from incremental energy conditions that are, at the differentiable level, essentially equivalent to the Sym/skew conclusions (the paper itself notes this equivalence in Section 3.2). The genuinely nontrivial content is the incidence wiring from (L)+(P)+(O) in Lemma B.4; the framing that port-Hamiltonian structure is 'deduced rather than assumed' oversells what is assumed versus derived.

Generality of the empirical validation is narrower than the framing suggests. Nearly all quantitative benchmarks are wave/oscillator-type systems with canonical (q, p) structure and diagonal SPD metrics (linear waves, damped waves, FPU, sine-Gordon, Duffing-type lattices, spring elasticity). The theory restricts states to pairs of adjacent-degree cochains, which excludes advection, transport, and general fluid settings where MGN-type models are most used. The single The Well experiment (acoustic scattering) is the only less-canonical test and is limited to a subset with modest experimental detail.

Some claims outrun the evidence: 'near-zero energy drift' in Table 2 is 1.3e-4 for MeshFT-Net, and OOD drifts in Table 5/11 are ~1e-3 to 1e-1 — small relative to baselines but not near zero; conclusions should be stated relative to baselines rather than as absolute fidelity claims.

Baseline fairness is mostly careful, but the paper primarily uses pedagogically simple baselines (MGN, MGN-HP, HNN, FNO, GraphCON, PI-MGN) at similar training budgets; stronger structure-preserving competitors from the DEC/data-driven-DEC literature (e.g., Trask et al. 2022-style learned Hodge networks) are discussed in related work but not compared against empirically.

Error propagation and statistical reporting are inconsistent across sections: some tables report seeds and std (Table 11), others only means; several OOD entries are capped at '> 100' without clearer divergence statistics, and the The Well experiment uses a single dataset configuration with limited robustness analysis.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section. Important scope restrictions (adjacent-degree cochain states, state-independent J in the main experiments, diagonal/block-diagonal metric parameterization, applicability to non-Hamiltonian/advection-dominated PDEs) are scattered in remarks rather than consolidated for the reader.

strengths: The core idea—separating topological (incidence-wired) structure from metric-dependent constitutive factors in mesh-based learned dynamics—is clean and well-motivated, connecting DEC, port-Hamiltonian theory, and graph-based simulators in a principled way.

The local reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) and its supporting lemmas are clearly stated, with a reasonably complete proof in Appendix B, and the ablation studies (Tables 7, 8, 14) directly probe which structural assumptions matter empirically.

The experimental suite is broad in kind: one-step and rollout accuracy, energy drift, physics-consistency diagnostics (dispersion, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum), OOD shifts, data-efficiency curves, and computational cost, which goes beyond what many structure-preserving learning papers report.

The MeshFT-Net architecture (fixed skew incidence interconnection + learned SPD metric/dissipation with a KDK/Strang integrator) is simple, cheap (642 parameters vs. ~10^5 for baselines), and the reported latency/memory profile is favorable.

The paper is generally well organized, with honest per-benchmark discussion (e.g., acknowledging MGN's lower one-step MSE on the dissipative benchmark) and a dedicated analysis of when state-dependent conservative coupling is needed (Section 5.7).
weaknesses: The central theorem is close to tautological as stated: Assumption (E) imposes incremental (two-point) power-balance conditions for all state pairs, which are essentially the infinitesimal version of the conclusion. Lemma B.3 deriving the skew/dissipative split from these conditions is a standard argument, and the genuinely new content (incidence wiring of J) rests on Lemma B.1/B.2, whose linearity assumption is only justified informally. The 'principle-driven deduction' claim is therefore weaker than advertised.

The evaluation is heavily circular: the primary benchmarks (planar waves on periodic grids, damped waves, wave-equation consistency tests) are generated by dynamics that lie exactly inside the MeshFT-Net hypothesis class (linear wave dynamics with incidence-wired coupling). Strongly outperforming MGN/HNN/FNO on data sampled from its own model class demonstrates the constraint but not broad usefulness; the more realistic tests (The Well subset, heterogeneous elasticity) are narrower, and the The Well experiment uses only one-step teacher forcing with an ad hoc sponge layer.

Baseline fairness is questionable: baselines use hidden width 64 with 4 layers (~10^5-10^6 parameters) while MeshFT-Net has 642 parameters, and baselines such as MGN exhibit implausibly poor results (energy drift 25.9 in Table 2, TSMSE > 100 across many benchmarks). This pattern suggests under-tuned or mismatched baselines rather than a pure architectural effect, and no tuning budget or hyperparameter search protocol is reported.

Novelty relative to prior work is limited: Trask et al. (2022) already fix discrete incidence operators and learn metric-dependent Hodge stars, and structure-preserving mesh/Hamiltonian learning is well developed. The paper's claimed distinction—that the structure is 'deduced' rather than postulated—hinges on the theorem whose assumptions substantially encode the conclusion.
Reproducibility claims are undermined: the abstract ends with the dangling sentence 'The code is available at' with no actual link, and no supplementary artifact is evident.

Several references have implausible or future-dated details (e.g., Hernández et al., 2026; He et al., 2026, TMLR 2026; PNAS 123(20), 2026), which raises concerns about citation accuracy and care in preparation.

Limitations are not candidly discussed: the paper does not acknowledge that (i) the state-independent-incidence restriction may exclude important physics (addressed only via a small ablation), (ii) nonlinear PDEs with non-quadratic energies are only lightly tested, and (iii) the quadratic first-order model used throughout experiments (G_theta state-independent) is a substantial restriction relative to the general theorem.

Some reported results lack uncertainty or statistical treatment (e.g., Table 2 reports means over 3 seeds with no variance), and several tables use display caps ('>100') that obscure the magnitude of baseline divergence.

strengths: The central idea is well motivated and clearly articulated: separating topological structure (fixed signed-incidence interconnection) from metric structure (learned Hodge-like operators) in mesh-based learned simulators, grounded in the DEC observation that d is topological while the Hodge star is metric-dependent.

The paper provides a genuine theory-to-architecture pipeline: Theorem 3.3 derives (rather than assumes) the port-Hamiltonian factorization from four stated principles, and MeshFT-Net is a direct implementation of the fixed-vs-learnable split identified by the theorem. The appendix proof chain (Lemmas B.1–B.4) is structured and mostly coherent.

Empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: analytic plane-wave benchmarks on grids and Delaunay meshes, dissipative benchmarks, physics-consistency diagnostics (wave speed, canonical consistency, PDE residuals, equipartition, momentum), OOD shifts (frequency, resolution, wave speed), a transfer test on The Well acoustic scattering, nonlinear lattices (FPU, damped phi^4, sine-Gordon), scalability/cost analysis, and multiple targeted ablations (topology-metric separation, state-dependent coupling, and principle-level ablations selectively violating each assumption).

The ablations are well designed and directly test the theorem's claims: breaking topology or orientation causes large energy/momentum drift, violating metric positivity breaks energy balance, and learned-J variants underperform incidence-assembled J even with comparable one-step MSE. This is the strongest evidence that the structure, not capacity, drives the gains.
Reproducibility is good: code release is promised, hyperparameters, data generation, and metric definitions are detailed in the appendix, and multiple seeds are reported.
weaknesses: The reduction theorem's reach is narrower than the framing suggests. It is a local, Jacobian-level statement only; no global port-Hamiltonian dynamics are established. Moreover, the strict convexity requirement G(z) ≻ 0 excludes degenerate/constrained systems (incompressible flow, gauge constraints beyond the Hamiltonian case) and the incremental two-point energy conditions in Assumption (E) are strong — Lemma B.3 largely extracts the skew/dissipative split directly from them, so the substantive content of the theorem is mostly the incidence-wiring step (Lemma B.4), whose proof is terse and somewhat heuristic (the step from skew-symmetry plus shared per-relation-type weights to exactly diagonal Ck with the stated block factorization is not fully verified).

The experimental evidence is largely generated from data whose structure is matched to the model's hypothesis class: linear waves, spring lattices, and Rayleigh-damped oscillators are all instances of the assumed port-Hamiltonian incidence form, so MeshFT-Net's dominant advantage is close to guaranteed by construction. The only genuinely out-of-template data is the acoustic-scattering subset of The Well, and no truly non-Hamiltonian physics (advection-dominated flows, Navier-Stokes) is tested, leaving the method's generality claim under-supported.

Some baselines appear under-optimized: MGN and MGN-HP use modest capacities and one-step training, and several OOD entries diverge (>100), which inflates relative gaps. A tuned state-of-the-art learned simulator comparison would strengthen the significance claims.

Reported results are not uniformly favorable and are occasionally glossed over: under the wave-speed OOD shift, MeshFT-Net's TSMSE (7.1e-1) is worse than HNN and FNO; the monotonicity-violation rate on the damped phi^4 benchmark (3.25e-1) is high; and FPU results are second-best to HNN. These limitations deserve more prominent discussion.

Presentation has a number of defects that should be fixed before acceptance: the abstract's code URL is incomplete ('The code is available at'), typos ('metrix', 'other thatn', 'though the lens', 'relying the reduction theorem'), inconsistent notation usage between Theorem 3.3 (J_k,k+1 = -D⊤C_k) and the incidence-normalized form used in experiments, and a garbled Table 4(b) column header (9.999 96 × 10−1).

The claim that starting from principles 'avoids committing to a single global template, which improves robustness to model mismatch' is asserted but not directly tested; the model-mismatch regime where the true dynamics fall outside the incidence form is exactly the untested regime noted above.
